title: Samuel Sokota (@ssokota) — thread (16 tweets)
summary:
[1/16] SOTA AI for games like poker & Hanabi rely on search methods that don’t scale to games w/ large amounts of hidden information.
In our ICLR paper, we introduce simple search methods that scale to large games & get SOTA for Hanabi w/ 100x less compute. 1/N
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GJq4S-gWkAAtnY1.jpg
────────
[2/16] These aforementioned poker & Hanabi AIs do search using objects known as public belief states (PBSs).
How do these PBS methods work? And what makes them fundamentally unscalable? 2/N
────────
[3/16] The rough idea is similar to search for perfect-information games:
1) Construct a subgame.
2) Determine a good policy for the subgame. 3/N
────────
[4/16] However, step 1) differs between perfect-info games & imperfect-info games.
With perfect info, constructing subgames is straightforward (eg, for Go, start the game from the current board).
In contrast, with imperfect info, it’s not obvious how to handle hidden information. 4/N
────────
[5/16] PBS methods address this issue by using subgames that include every decision point consistent with public knowledge.
In Texas Hold’em, this means that each subgame involves not only the hand the search player was actually dealt, but also every other conceivable hand. 5/N
────────
[6/16] Because there are only 52 choose 2 hands in Texas Hold’em, the search player can reason about all of these hands.
However, as the amount of hidden information grows, this approach quickly becomes infeasible. 6/N
────────
[7/16] Thus, alternative frameworks are required to scale search to games with large amounts of hidden information.
In our ICLR paper, we present such a framework that we call the framework of update equivalence. 7/N
────────
[8/16] The core idea is simple: replicate the updates of last-iterate algorithms with desirable properties, such as improvements in expected return, decreases in exploitability, or convergence to an equilibrium. 8/N
────────
[9/16] Since last-iterate algorithms do not typically rely on PBSs, the framework of update equivalence scales naturally to games with large amounts of hidden information. 9/N
────────
[10/16] Using this framework of update equivalence, we introduce a provably sound search algorithm for fully cooperative games based on mirror descent.
The algorithm works by estimating Q-values using rollouts and performing a mirror descent update on top of the estimated Q-values. 10/N
────────
[11/16] We test this algorithm, which we call mirror descent search (MDS), in Hanabi—the most competitive benchmark for search in cooperative games.
We show MDS exceeds or matches the performance of PBS methods while using 100x less search time. 11/N
────────
[12/16] This performance gap widens as the amount of hidden information increases, reflecting MDS’s superior scalability compared to PBS methods. 12/N
────────
[13/16] We also introduce a similar algorithm for adversarial games based on magnetic mirror descent (see thread below) & show it improves performance in games with virtually no public information, where PBS methods are essentially inapplicable. 13/N
Quoting @ssokota
A longstanding disappointment in multi-agent research has been that naive self-play RL fails in adversarial games.
In our ICLR paper, we present a simple principled approach that enables self-play RL to succeed in such settings. 1/N
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/ext_tw_video_thumb/1650781546830344193/pu/img/A8SeXh9rw8wY-mI8.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/ext_tw_video/1650781546830344193/pu/vid/480x270/TMIyxiYVulatn5xU.mp4?tag=12
────────
[14/16] Overall, our results suggest that the update-equivalence framework opens the door to effective search in games with large amounts of hidden information. 14/N
────────
[15/16] If you are interested in learning more, reach out with questions, check out the paper below, or come chat at ICLR. 15/N
────────
[16/16] Thanks to @MetaAI for supporting this research, which was conducted during an internship supervised by @polynoamial in collaboration with @gabrfarina, @lightvector1, @HengyuanH, @often_wang, and @zicokolter. N/N

title: Samuel Sokota (@ssokota) — thread (10 tweets)
summary:
[1/10] Maximizing mutual information (MI) is a fundamental problem.
We’re releasing a package for approximately maximizing MI between any two discrete distributions.
This package enables high-throughput perfectly secure steganography with language models. 1/N
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/GP3UiruXMAAaA8b.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/tweet_video/GP3UiruXMAAaA8b.mp4
────────
[2/10] What is steganography?
And how does maximizing mutual information enable it? 2/N
────────
[3/10] This is an idea we’ve been developing over a series of works.
It originated from a question @j_foerst formulated about whether it’s possible to communicate information through Markov decision process trajectories. 5/N
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/ext_tw_video_thumb/1800834381201674240/pu/img/jFWMZY5XXrLuEEeq.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/ext_tw_video/1800834381201674240/pu/vid/avc1/540x270/euHOP_z1Sm69gKJV.mp4?tag=12
────────
[4/10] We can do steganography by maximizing the mutual information between a distribution of innocuous content and a distribution of secret messages.
Encoding and decoding are performed using the associated conditional distributions. 4/N
────────
[5/10] Steganography is the practice of encoding secret information within seemingly innocuous content.
Like cryptography, it enables sending sensitive information over public channels.
But unlike cryptography, it hides the very fact that sensitive communication is taking place. 3/N
────────
[6/10] Most recently, in a paper to appear at UAI, we extended the approach to unencrypted secret messages, for which it’s possible to achieve high rates of information throughput, as shown in the video at the top of the thread. 7/N
────────
[7/10] The effectiveness of MI maximization for communication led us to investigate its security guarantees.
We proved that it is perfectly secure, meaning that it’s statistically impossible to detect, for encrypted secret messages. 6/N
────────
[8/10] These works were co-led by @casdewitt, in collaboration with @dylanjsam, Spencer Compton, @MaxiIgl, @luisa_zintgraf, @philiptorr, @shimon8282, @MasorX, @zicokolter, and @j_foerst. 9/N
────────
[9/10] This line of work was made possible by algorithms, such as that of @murat_kocaoglu_ et al. [2017], for minimum-entropy coupling, which is equivalent to MI maximization for two marginals, due to the equality below. 8/N
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GP3akSXWAAAJO7E.jpg
────────
[10/10] If you’re interested in learning more, check out our package and the papers below, reach out with questions, or come chat at UAI or ICML. N/N

title: Samuel Sokota (@ssokota) — thread (13 tweets)
summary:
[1/13] Model-free deep RL algorithms like NFSP, PSRO, ESCHER, & R-NaD are tailor-made for games with hidden information (e.g. poker).
We performed the largest-ever comparison of these algorithms.
We find that they do not outperform generic policy gradient methods, such as PPO. 1/N
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GjxFgEmXkAEi1Yk.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GjxFhceXAAARJsO.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GjxFje_XYAA5AoK.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GjxFkrfW8AALqda.jpg
────────
[2/13] Why have researchers been making bespoke deep RL algorithms for hidden-information games?
The reason is that naive self-play RL can fail catastrophically in the presence of hidden information. 2/N
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/ext_tw_video_thumb/1890462759101386752/pu/img/5ShrU2gozV6DB6v-.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/ext_tw_video/1890462759101386752/pu/vid/avc1/480x270/zw0f2QWaAp8cdKZr.mp4?tag=12
────────
[3/13] The success of MMD is cause for reflection.
Given the proximity between MMD and PPO, shouldn’t PPO (and other generic policy gradient algorithms) perform well, too?
Why, then, has PPO only appeared in literature as an underperforming baseline? 5/N
────────
[4/13] Recently, a surprising alternative approach emerged based on magnetic mirror descent (MMD).
Despite being a standard policy gradient algorithm, MMD achieves strong performance in hidden-information games. 4/N
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GjxGExRW0AAx0s4.jpg
────────
[5/13] Bespoke deep RL algorithms can avert this failure by building on methods with convergence guarantees, like fictitious play, double oracle, & counterfactual regret minimization.
But they often suffer from implementation complexity, slow convergence, & scalability challenges. 3/N
────────
[6/13] Over 5600 total runs, we find that NFSP, PSRO, ESCHER and R-NaD fail to outperform generic policy gradient algorithms like MMD, PPO, and PPG, both in terms of exploitability and head-to-head matchups. 9/N
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GjxGydCWQAAWSSv.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GjxG04TWcAAJFon.jpg
────────
[7/13] We address this issue by implementing efficient exploitability computations for 4 games millions of times larger than standard benchmarks.
Using these games, we conduct the largest-ever exploitability comparison of DRL algorithms for hidden-information games. 8/N
────────
[8/13] The standard measure of performance (exploitability) is difficult to efficiently implement for large games.
This issue has plagued the field, forcing researchers to resort to tenuous metrics, thus making progress difficult to measure. 7/N
────────
[9/13] We hypothesize that generic policy gradient algorithms like PPO are fully capable of achieving competitive or superior performance for hidden-information games, given appropriate tuning.
However, resolving this hypothesis is not straightforward. 6/N
────────
[10/13] To address this, we release our exploitability implementations in a package compatible with OpenSpiel, the most widely used library for RL in games.
To play the benchmark games, check out the demo @nathanlichtle made. 11/N
────────
[11/13] What should we make of this?
One takeaway is that the field has suffered from a lack of suitable benchmarks. 10/N
────────
[12/13] This project was a collaboration with @maxbrudolph, @nathanlichtle, @___sobhan___, @alexandrebayen, @zicokolter, @yayitsamyzhang, @gabrfarina, and @EugeneVinitsky.
For more, check out the paper below or reach out with questions. N/N
────────
[13/13] Beyond benchmarks, another, more aspirational, takeaway is that we are closer than ever to the ideal of a single simple deep policy gradient algorithm that works universally across games.
We think this is an ideal worth pursuing. 12/N

title: Samuel Sokota (@ssokota) — thread (9 tweets)
clean_title: Ataraxos: the first superhuman AI for Stratego and other imperfect information games
summary:
[1/9] In our Nature paper, we introduce the first superhuman Stratego AI, which we built using general techniques that we developed for RL & test-time compute under imperfect information. 1/N
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTe7SV7akAE3q3L.png
────────
[2/9] Imperfect information makes it difficult to design effective RL & test-time compute approaches because the value of an action depends not only on the policies employed thereafter, but also on the policies employed prior to and at the time of that action. 2/N
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTe6atAaMAABLCc.jpg
────────
[3/9] In our paper, we establish general regularization-based approaches to RL & test-time compute that are scalable to settings with large amounts of hidden information. 4/N
────────
[4/9] Poker AI research led to the development of techniques that can sidestep this issue when there is a small amount of hidden information, but settings with large amounts of hidden information remained challenging. 3/N
────────
[5/9] Due to the large amount of hidden information, Stratego had been among the last major competitively played board games at which humans had remained superior to AI, and was the subject of a significant DeepMind research effort, whose work we built upon. 6/N
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTe6uOTa4AAzBSg.jpg
────────
[6/9] We used these approaches to build Ataraxos, the first superhuman AI for Stratego. In an official 20-game series, Ataraxos defeated Pim Niemeijer, the most decorated player of all time, with a 15W-1L-4D record; it also went 38W-2L against 2025 world championship attendees. 5/N
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTe52kXbgAAsaA9.jpg
────────
[7/9] For many details, including a purely GPU-based RL loop and data-filtering scheme that increased our sample-efficiency, compute-efficiency, and asymptotic performance, see the paper or codebase linked below. N/N
────────
[8/9] This project was a multi-year collaboration with @EugeneVinitsky, @HengyuanH, @nanomena0, @zicokolter, and @gabrfarina, over which time we found numerous tricks that allowed us to succeed despite being limited to academic levels of compute. 8/N
────────
[9/9] We also used the approaches we developed to build the first superhuman AI for Barrage Stratego, which defeated 3 world champions in 50-game series, and state-of-the-art AIs for Hanabi and dou dizhu, demonstrating applicability across adversarial, cooperative, and team games. 7/N
clean_summary:
Stratego is a board game with a lot of hidden information, making it hard for AI to plan effectively because the value of an action depends on unknown past and current policies. Previous poker AI techniques worked well with little hidden information but struggled with games like Stratego.

Samuel Sokota and collaborators developed general regularization methods for reinforcement learning and test-time compute that scale to large hidden information. Their AI, Ataraxos, beat the top human player 15-1 with 4 draws and dominated world championship attendees. They also applied these methods to Barrage Stratego, Hanabi, and dou dizhu, showing the approach works across different game types. Details and code are available on GitHub.
